children: Bank of America investors were hit with two problems at once Wednesday: a
$1.2 billion regulatory penalty
and an earnings report that still looked soft even after stripping that charge out.
Shares of Bank of America
fell more than
, their steepest daily decline since April 2025, after the bank reported third-quarter earnings of
$0.91 per share
, down from $1.04 a year earlier. The regulatory charge reduced EPS by about
The fine itself was unusually large.
The U.S. Treasury said Bank of America will pay more than
$1.21 billion
over failures involving anti-money-laundering controls and sanctions compliance, making it the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. Regulators said the bank failed to timely report more than
$5 billion in suspicious transactions
, including over $1 billion tied to priority illicit-finance risks.
But the market reaction goes beyond one expensive settlement.
Excluding the fine, Bank of America earned about
$1.08 per share
, still below the roughly $1.10 analysts expected. Trading revenue fell 5% to about
$5.1 billion
, while investment-banking fees dropped 11% to $1.8 billion.
The regulatory problem is bigger than the cash charge
Treasury's findings point to deficiencies that developed over years rather than a single mistake.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency imposed a
record $750 million penalty
, saying Bank of America's anti-money-laundering program remained deficient even after a 2024 cease-and-desist order required improvements.
The bank must now work with an independent third party to review past transactions and identify suspicious activity that may have gone undetected.
That matters because the financial cost does not necessarily end with the fine.
Additional compliance spending, outside reviews and remediation work can weigh on expenses well after the original penalty disappears from the income statement.

title: Bank of America Selloff Goes Beyond $1.2 Billion Penalty
